description: Daymon, a dissipated man who abused his wife, was arrested and charged with murdering her in Beargrass Creek, where a wooden boot and a chintz calico dress matching her attire were found. The indictment formally charged him with murder in the first degree. Despite claiming not guilty, Daymon had no defense appointed, and the state presented circumstantial evidence, including witness testimony and the discovery of the body, to a jury that returned a guilty verdict. The trial occurred in a crowded courtroom, with the judge, a crippled man, observing the proceedings and pausing to gaze at the prisoner. Beargrass Creek, which flows into the Ohio River near Louisville, had long been a site of quiet solitude, now disrupted by steam navigation, which alarmed wildlife and broke the stillness around early settler graves. Old heroes who fought for free river navigation had requested burial along the Ohio, where the music of the steam engine would soothe their spirits, a desire fulfilled as the river remained navigable.

Governor Morock, a retired Chicago lawyer known for handling dirty work, received one thousand dollars from Cousin Caesar to assist in a legal dispute over the Simon estate in Arkansas. He affirmed that money can prove anything, including mental faculties, and claimed he could secure two to three hundred bales of cotton worth four hundred dollars each—described as "nothing but a crumb." Roxie Daymon, who believed she was the only witness at the time, sought his help after hearing that Caesar Simon planned to break Young Simon’s will. Morock calculated the suit’s cost, which included witnesses, and failed to collect any scraps from the burned Simon plantation despite spending the thousand dollars. Cliff Carlo, a family representative and southern army veteran, was in close counsel with Cousin Caesar about the legal expenses, though he was non-committal. The Simon estate, valued over a million and a quarter, was eventually sold at sheriff’s sale. Morock now lives off his bad reputation, and society in Shirt-Tail Bend began to improve after the war.

Tom Fairfield, from one of Virginia's best families, ran away at twelve and traveled to Kentucky in 1791 with a group of emigrants who settled near Boone Station. He developed a restless spirit and, inspired by the joyous spring days, decided to become a preacher, believing reading sufficed for understanding Scripture. Kentucky, known as "The Dark and Bloody Ground" by Indigenous peoples due to violent conflicts between settlers and Native tribes, had a male-dominated population due to female reluctance amid ongoing warfare. Weddings featured the custom of "running for the bottle," a race on fine horses involving fifteen to twenty young men, where a bottle of corn whisky was offered to the first to reach. Early settlers held religious and love feasts in the woods near streams, lasting days or weeks. Tom sought to improve his social standing through preaching, but faced financial hardship. In a later incident, he was served spoiled beer by Dave at a store, which caused a violent reaction, leading to his expulsion.

Roxie Daymon, a young and beautiful woman full of life and vigor, consented to marry a dying man, silencing the Good Angel of Observation, who had previously failed to detect her feelings. This marriage contrasts with the view that a young man prioritizes fame and fortune, focusing mental energy on wealth and seeing his wife as a convenience. Daymon, a laborer who frequently assisted in navigating boats across the falls, was dissipated and abused his wife in fits of intoxication. His wife, described as young, intelligent, and pure, was missing from Louisville, with no known relatives. The passage notes that marriage is the most important life step, and while same temperaments lead to children inheriting bad qualities, opposites are more likely to produce children with good qualities. A separate incident involves Tom, who placed Suza Fairfield, a child, in his covered wagon between his dirty children, giving her a gag and commanding his wife to silence her if she made noise, then drove south through dense fog.

Suza, after weeping, used her good sense to trace the creek south to a ford and retrace it north to the river, doubling her task, recalling Aunt Katy’s phrase "if there is a will, there is a way." She traveled for two hours along the creek’s zigzag path, waded through shallow water (one foot deep), and reached a big road where she recognized the ford from her prior passage in the prison wagon. On the north side, she saw the dark woods and a friendly road, deciding to follow it to Port William even if Tom Ditamus caught her. The Mississippi River was bank full and carried drift wood during a foggy fall morning when the Western hemisphere blindfolded the eye of day. A country school, built from round logs and using drift wood from the Ohio River for benches, provided basic education to Roxie. Cousin Cæsar, hardened by early hardships, was likened to drift wood, while the Roman Eagle moved swiftly downstream through the river’s dark, muddy waters.

Brindle Bill, a wood-chopper and leading spirit of his party, was part of a scheme to swindle Don Carlo at headquarters, where a tallow candle illuminated a pile of silver dollars. After being insulted by Don Carlo, Brindle Bill claimed the money and declared he would fight S. S. Simon, a contest settled by physical strength and ending when the vanquished cried "enough." Personal quarrels were rare and resolved by early boatmen’s rules requiring unarmed, fair fights. Brindle Bill was seen as a bully due to his strength and stories of past combats. The country suffered widespread abuse, with crops ravaged, cotton burned—by both the southern commander to prevent enemy capture and unknown hands—and palaces destroyed by torch. In a separate scene, Tom and his family endured a long, cold winter, with the cold wind the only sound as they sat by a tallow candle telling stories. Woodmen ran out of cabins with torches to show the first light after a steamboat rang for wood.

Port William, the first settlement at the mouth of the Kentucky River, was a hub of whisky trade and social activity, with corn whisky distilled in the upper counties and shipped via keel boats, later known as old Bourbon. Dave Deminish operated a saloon initially called a grocery, where cheap John merchandise and whisky were sold; Redhead Sam Sims ran a whisky shop and tavern. Old Brother Demitt owned land and slaves and was a church leader, while Old Arch Wheataker owned slaves, rode his ball-face sorrel horse, and drank whisky daily, returning home on Old Ball, which once frightened him and broke his head. The Angel of Observation looked into the back room of Dave Deminish on a dark night in late December, and observed a party that won their last dime and fell asleep except for Suza Fairfield, an eleven-year-old orphan who told stories of abuse by Aunt Katy, declared she would escape her, and fled to Port William with a lazy ox team, following the Kentucky River. Suza and Don Carlo were engaged, and phrases like latch-string and pack-horse, once familiar to grandfathers, are now obsolete.

The Governor, a liberal and secretive figure, offers to handle legal matters for a stake of one thousand dollars, with additional fees up to a million, claiming the work is costly due to complexity and that breaking a will would bring financial gain despite its expense. He suggests using legal loopholes, such as arranging a shadow marriage for fifty dollars, and equates "picking up the crumbs" with securing small benefits. Cousin Cæsar, well-informed about family circumstances from a descendant of Brindle Bill, knows of a will involving twenty thousand dollars with twenty years interest against an estate, and that Roxie Daymon is an heir. Young Simon, a wealthy cotton planter who died in the city, left his estate—worth over a million dollars—to Roxie, who expresses caution, wanting to see how a dead man’s shoes will fit before accepting benefits. The Demitt kinsfolk speculate about Aunt Katy’s money, hoping to inherit when she dies, believing a will favors Suza Fairfield. The case is later taken to the Supreme Court, which denies a monopolist’s claim to navigate western waters by steam. Roxie ultimately rejects the Governor’s counsel, asserting she has no further need for a lawyer.

Steve Brindle, a private in General Pearce’s army from Arkansas, saved Cousin Cæsar from bleeding to death on a battlefield after discovering him wounded by a musket ball. A Cherokee Indian, belonging to General McCulloch’s army, assisted by applying ashes from a campfire to the wound. Steve bound the injury and stopped the blood, then carried Cousin Cæsar to camp where he recovered. Steve and the Cherokee Indian were searching the battlefield when they found Cousin Cæsar, who had crawled a quarter of a mile before collapsing from blood loss. Steve shared his family history with Cousin Cæsar, opening the door to wealth, though Cousin Cæsar later concealed Steve’s antecedents. Steve had encoded a message on a card referencing "No. 77" in Chicago, which only Cousin Cæsar understood, indicating Steve had deserted the steam carriage—interpreted as a coded signal. Cousin Cæsar remained uncertain whether Steve wanted him to follow. After the incident, the two men were hired as boat hands.

Brindle Bill, known as Bill, was a former resident of Shirt-Tail Bend who left to work chopping wood to raise money for a new start, having been three times removed from steamboats for playing three card monte. He recalled Susan La-s-co, the name of Simon’s wife’s mother, and believed he had discovered a lead: twenty thousand in bank, left by an Englishman after the burning of the Brandywine, with Rose Simon as heir. At Sundown Hill, a conversation revealed that the Carlo wood yard had ended, Don Carlo had returned to Kentucky and was blown up on a steamboat, and Simon had changed since Hill last saw him, now making pretensions to be a planter. Bill advised Hill to go slow, citing a hen on the nest, and claimed he came back to play a strong game with the twenty thousand in bank, winking to indicate he dealt and the other played his cards. Bill believed Simon would never return and stated there was no mistake because uncle John had the di-dapper eggs in his pocket. S. S. Simon, obsessed with dying rich, died from hard work and exposure, with no thought of death.

Cæsar Simon, a soldier in Gen. Price’s Missouri campaign, was brave and joyful on the battlefield, eating roasted ears with invigorating spirit and focusing solely on southern victory. He thought little of Gov. Morock or the Simon estate, experiencing only sober second thoughts and self-reproach when facing the struggle for his life. The army, under Gen. Price, marched over eight hundred miles, fought constantly, and began without money, wagons, cartridges, or bayonet-guns, later acquiring supplies from the Federals. It remained cheerful despite lack of food, pay, or clothing, dancing bare-footed and ragged around campfires. The campaign included the hard-fought battle at Oak Hill (Springfield), where federal troops under Gen. Lyon faced about eleven thousand Confederate troops led by McCulloch, Price, and Pearce. After Gen. Lyon’s death, Confederates gained control. Gen. Van Dorn ordered a rash retreat, sending the sick ahead. Cæsar Simon left Kentucky for Missouri to consult with the Carlo family about property interests, stating he had made his decision and would stand the hazard. He fell in battle, becoming the last male in the Simon family line.

Alonzo Phelps, convicted of murder and sentenced to hanging, escaped from jail by knocking down the jailer with a stone ink-stand and wrote a confession stating he first murdered a man in Europe, fleeing for safety before coming to America. He concealed a bundle of papers at the site of the burial, which were later found through his confession and restored the family’s fortune, which had been held in abeyance due to their loss. John A. Lasco, who remained behind in Europe, considered Susan Lasco the last family link and made her inheritance his last will. Susan and their father emigrated to America, leaving John behind. Rose Simon, Susan’s cousin, received the news with delight and identified a breast-pin inscribed "Presented to Susan Lasco by her brother, John A. Lasco, 1751" as proof of kinship. Brindle Bill testified that Rose Simon was the only surviving child of Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco. Rose died of yellow fever in New Orleans. Cousin Cæsar arranged for her remains to be transported to Arkansas and placed beside the father on the family plantation. Young Simon, a cotton planter, inherited four plantations and over 600 slaves.

Rose and Roxie Fairfield are sisters, the children of Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco, separated at Port William, the mouth of the Kentucky River. Rose, the younger, was raised by Mrs. Evaline Estep, who gave her a box of family keepsakes in exchange for taking the youngest orphan child. Roxie, the eldest, learned from her only known relative, Aunt Patsey Perkins, that her mother had two sisters, Rose and Suza, whom she called "poor trash." Roxie, shivering in the snow, sought help from Aunt Katy, who recognized her and confirmed her mother’s identity. Rose claims she has not heard from her sisters since more than fifteen years ago. S. S. Simon, seeking to manage a business, presents a certificate of deposit for twenty thousand dollars, arguing that gaps in records would reduce funds to less than seven thousand, preventing a fine house. Simon deceives Rose by claiming debts, pays Brindle Bill and Sundown Hill three hundred dollars each, and obtains her promise to allow him to manage the business. Aunt Fillis Foster is designated to take Roxie, while Mrs. Estep becomes Rose’s foster mother. Simon later suffers from swamp fever and is delirious, seeing Roxie repeatedly.

The narrator, a diligent observer and reader, undertook a survey tour with two <DW64> boys aged fifteen to twenty, leaving Bush Bayou—20 miles below Helena and 15 miles back from the Mississippi River—on the 14th of May to attend races starting at 12 o'clock on the 15th. The races, held one quarter of a mile for a stake of one hundred dollars, were soon after the inauguration of steam navigation on the Mississippi River. The Bayou, an old bed of the great river, featured large trees extending across its width and open spaces up to a mile long. The narrator spotted and bridled a mule with disputed origins—claimed to have been ridden from northern Mexico by the first Chickasaw Frenchman or part of First Napoleon’s army—using it to arrive at the race ground fifteen minutes early. The Spotted Buck won the race, though many believed it was a jockey race and that Silver Heels was the fastest. The narrator, comparing himself to Roman Cæsar, observed human behavior and societal traps, noting that gamblers and thieves operate on the same theory. He obtained the Governor of Arkansas’s signature on a land grant and title to a tract of land, entering events like a log cabin without ringing a bell.

Cole Conway, at twenty years old and living in Paducah, Kentucky, was in partnership with Steve Sharp, with whom he played a card game involving a dream in which the last card, thick and resembling a box, contained gold pieces. After Conway placed the money in his pocket and waited for Sharp to claim half, Sharp dismissed the cards as being for men who sell prize cards. When Conway retrieved the money, something strange occurred. Steve Sharp and Cole Conway both crawled into an old straw shed in the suburbs of the village, where they slept, with the sun having crossed the meridian on the other side of the globe. Brindle Bill, who claimed bad luck and lost all his money, winked his right eye and told Simon to find where the division of orphan children took place, as he was raised there and the rest of the children are dead. Simon, a man between honest and rogue, paid Brindle Bill three hundred dollars. Daymon, a day laborer, worked in the infant city and accepted a deed to fifteen acres of land after Roxie persuaded him to stay. A land-holder was indebted to Daymon for one hundred and fifty dollars, having endured hard labor and practiced strict economy. Daymon later sold one acre for more than the whole tract and began selling by the foot. Wild ducks were present near the lake and voiced the deep, dead hour, awakening Don Carlo.

Don and Dan Carlo are close brothers with differing attitudes; Dan is a fast friend of Brindle Bill and receives half the money from wood business sales, while Don covers all expenses and repeatedly urges Dan to show family pride, a promise Dan consistently fails to keep. Don and Dan share a long-standing partnership in the wood business, marked by financial strain and failed appeals. Simon's wife, a quiet but influential figure, observes the conflict, hears blows and blood during a fight between Don and Brindle Bill, and sets the cabin on fire with a fire-brand before friction matches were invented, ending the contest with Don Carlo winning the money. She sees Don Carlo approaching headquarters and anticipates trouble. Don inherited strength from his mother, while Dan was born to be a rake. A relative on the mother's side held land title papers granting Don and Dan Carlo rights to establish a wood yard. Tom and his wife, whom he called "mother," discussed family fortune and poverty, with Tom’s wife hoping for revival through ancestral papers. Young Simon, heir to a large estate, knew little of his family history.

Cousin Cæsar, known as "big-sis" for being the eldest, was raised by two penniless sisters and cared for cousin Cæsar's childhood. He showed imaginative behavior by expecting bubbles on the suds to burst into a loaf of bread, prompting "big-sis" to give him a loaf of bread with butter as a reward for imagination. Young Simon, Cæsar's cousin, grew up without hardships or good health, lacking a family name and being almost as poor as his slaves; he was ignorant of his father's history, with the name Roxie Daymon making a lasting impression. He was mischievous and alternated between living with "big-sis" and "little-sis," who initially whipped him, until "little-sis" improved the discipline. Cæsar Simon, the son of S. S. Simon who died in early life in West Tennessee, left three children, including Cæsar. A born soldier, Cæsar Simon was driven by battle and resolved to die in the last ditch, calling Steve Brindle a coward. General Lyon attacked them before sunrise, was wounded twice, and was shot dead leading a rash charge during the battle. The Cherokee Indian who saved Cæsar was drawn into war by Albert Pike.

Tom, a six-foot-tall man with square shoulders, a forty-five-degree forehead retreat, a large skull, and a dark shade in his eye, is described as cowardly and lazy, intending to return to his old home in a covered wagon. His wife, a "pussy-cat woman" who obeys his commands without considering woman's rights, attends meetings with him of the New Lights sect. During church services, when the preacher's earnestness warms the congregation, the "jerks" begin—starting slowly and becoming spasmodic or rapid—mainly affecting females, causing loss of discretion, loss of modesty, and people jerking themselves onto the floor. Tom's wife is attacked by the jerks, resulting in her combs flying and her long black hair cracking like a wagon whip; Tom is frightened and, with friends' help, she is taken home and becomes quiet. The jerks are primarily experienced by females but occasionally affect men. Tom and his wife attend all meetings with the intention of achieving a specific objective.

Rob Roy was a bachelor wood cutter who lived alone in a cabin made of three poles on Old Smith's land, where he kept his ax always polished and worked faithfully during the week, drinking whisky on Sundays. His cabin had a straw-filled sleeping couch made of three parallel poles, a three-legged stool, and a pine goods box. He never wore stockings or a coat. Old Smith’s land, described as fertile and forested with black walnut, cherry, and grape vines, is known as the garden of Kentucky. Cousin Cæsar, who detested work, stole Roy’s whisky jug, replaced it with cider, and was later caught and discharged by Old Smith after Roy refused to work. The cabin also housed other wood cutters, including Brindle Bill from Shirt-Tail Bend. A speaker emigrated in search of his sister Susan Lasco, who likely married and changed her name, leaving $20,000 on deposit in a western bank and $110 to the good woman of the house, who is to dry, preserve, and deliver the papers to a lawyer in Memphis. The speaker died without further directions.

Joe, a <DW52> boy, drove a wood slide through the snow with orphan girls Roxie and Rose, using a long switch to keep the old horse, Old Ned, ahead of the slide. Dick, an old <DW64> with severe gout in his left foot, could not wear a shoe and had his left foot wrapped in a saddle blanket, leaving an impression in the snow about the size of an elephant’s track. Dick placed a straw bed on the slide and caught Roxie, placing her on it while holding back the slide, but was too slow for the trip. Joe returned with Suza, the baby, who was placed in the middle of the slide, with Roxie and Rose on either side. Aunt Katy, who had a strong passion to save, watched the slide and remarked that Tom Fairfield was dead under the snow and that Old Demitt would try to poke one of the children on her. Joe had left home and moved to Canada, while life is described as a continuous, imperceptible change, with new men entering and old ones passing away every hour.

Shirt-Tail Bend, on the Mississippi River, was a settlement first established by woodcutters, where cord (steam wood) was the primary source of revenue, bringing thousands of dollars annually. The community lacked a schoolhouse, church, or post-office and operated with minimal infrastructure, governed by a rudimentary legal system. Brindle Bill, a strong and influential figure in the area, lived in Shirt-Tail Bend, was classified as part of the floating population, and died in state prison; he was the father of Steve Brindle, who described himself as a by-chance person. The area was marked by social contrasts, with Brindle Bill representing a spirit of degradation. The Enterprise steamboat, the first to ascend the Mississippi, landed in Louisville in May 1816 after a 25-day journey from New Orleans. B. F. Craig, author of "Pen Pictures," was born in the Ohio River region and spent his early life in the Mississippi woods, describing the social and natural life of the region. Louisville, located at the falls of the Ohio River, served as a key point on the river route between Pittsburgh and New Orleans.

The Ohio and Mississippi rivers, especially at night, posed dangerous conditions due to turbulent waters, drift wood, and darkness. Crossing the Mississippi with a heavily laden barque was deemed more perilous than encountering an alligator. The young narrator, brave and enthusiastic, directed the <DW64>s to stand still in the boat’s bottom to avoid being thrown overboard, and navigated safely toward a light in the cabin, landing at the Mississippi cabin. A large sixteen-foot alligator attacked the group, frightening the <DW64>s and prompting the narrator to fire a double-barreled shotgun with twenty-four buckshot, though the shot only glanced off the alligator’s scales. One of two girls rushed into the water and dragged something to shore, later confirmed as Don Carlo’s lifeless body, preventing his loss. Suza, walking in dark woods without a lamp, reached White’s creek, where an owl’s call caused her to weep. The land near the Kentucky and Ohio rivers narrows into a sharp point with deep, dark water. The dead and dying were collected and carried to nearby houses, and the shore saw widespread gathering of all classes.

The carriage featured a brass boiler with a slide door that revealed a dial showing both the time of day and the speed of the carriage. On the right side of the dial, a figure 77 made of India rubber was hung on a brass pin; each time the slide door was opened, one of the figure 7's fell off the pin, leading the operator to conclude the safe speed was seven miles per hour and to regulate the carriage to that speed. This pattern repeated consistently. Later, the carriage was running at fifteen miles per hour, despite no change in steam gauge, and a hissing sound indicated the water level was dropping. On the left side of the boiler, a brass handle resembling a pump handle was present; the operator seized it and began pumping, causing bubbling water. The operator maintained the speed of seven miles per hour based on the falling figure 77.

Gen. Sterling Price led an army composed of all classes of humanity, including mechanics, farmers, professionals, merchants, laborers, printers' devils, butchers, and deadbeats, who joined without pay or government support from the Confederate States of America. These citizens, aged 18 to 70, gathered double-barreled shot-guns from their communities and wore varied uniforms, from walnut roundabout to pigeon-tailed broadcloth. Motivated by a watchword similar to "To your tents, O Israeli," the unarmed and untrained army remained undefeated on Missouri soil during the first year of the war. Gov. Jackson fled Jefferson City as federal forces approached, and the Legislature convened in Neosho but could not assist Price. The so-called battle of Boonville was a reckless action by citizens not under Price’s command. Little Rock was the only place in the state with a resident who was a printers' devil or the author of a dime novel. The federal government at Washington announced it would never interfere with the slaves of loyal men.

In 1861, spring returned with softening breezes, marking a memorable season in Chicago. Young Simon and his cousin Cæsar arrived in Chicago via the iron horse, where Simon, living on excitement, found his source of life failing due to consumption. Cousin Cæsar carried him into a hotel, after which Simon never stood alone again; their marriage was postponed until his recovery. Roxie Daymon, a twenty-year-old woman known for her obedience and tidiness, had a lover and ran away with him, marrying by common law. They traveled to Louisville, where Daymon was granted a new trial that never occurred, before moving to Chicago. Roxie was admired for her wealth and presence at fashionable gatherings. The party of young people in Chicago, including Roxie, planned a trip to New Orleans, stopping briefly in the Crescent City before returning. The journey ended at the Simon plantations, where Simon was in the final stage of consumption and was traveling to the West Indies for winter. The proclamation of freedom by Lincoln removed slavery’s economic value on the Simon plantations. Brindle shared the narrative’s history with Cæsar, excluding Roxie’s story. Young Simon and Roxie were engaged to marry in Chicago the following spring.

Aunt Katy Demitt lives in Port William, Ohio, and owns a house with a chimney that has no smoke and a fire that has burned down; she is sleeping in her easy chair with her face buried in her hands. Suza Fairfield sees the house and recognizes her, gently calling her name, leading to an immediate embrace. Aunt Katy, who loves Suza deeply, reveals she has five hundred dollars in gold and silver and a will bequeathing all her possessions to Suza, witnessed by old Ballard and Father Tearful. Suza, captured by the Demitt relations, escapes on the first night, guided by Aunt Katy’s advice that "discretion is the better part of valor." Tom Ditamus, a restless boatman who traveled down the Kentucky River and up the Ohio River, was hired by the Demitts to take Suza to the backwoods, for ten dollars, believing her removal would silence her. After returning, Tom finds Suza gone and is indifferent, having obtained the Demitt money. The half-way castle, a brick house halfway between Louisville and Cincinnati, is mentioned in connection with Don Carlo’s fate. Old Demitt had one fault, but his kinsfolk had thousands; the estate passed to relatives except for Aunt Katy’s life interest.

Aunt Patsy Perkins is a prominent, style-conscious woman in Chicago who entertains with precision and is respected among the city’s elite for her rapid, thorough speech. She has no love for style and shares Old Perkins’s disdain for it, viewing his poor kin as burdensome, likening them to stumps in a flower garden. She is the aunt of Jim, an eighteen-year-old from Indiana who worked on the streets and was given occasional money by her, with instructions to avoid the house when she had company. She is known to be sharp and confrontational, declaring she will insult the first member of Old Perkins’s poor kin who enters her home if she cannot reach him. She receives a letter from Indiana about Cousin Sally, a plain, poor girl, and promises to make it hot for Old Perkins if she can talk. She is in conflict with Old Perkins, who is described as a "wooden man" and makes no impression on her. A servant announces her to Roxie in the Daymon palace, where Roxie reflects on childhood and Suza. Aunt Patsy later leaves the palace, vowing to study human nature. She is connected to events involving cousin Cæsar, who delivers a note to Governor Morock at No. 77 Strait Street, and to Roxie, who is left destitute after a will is discovered.

Price's Army camped on the southern border of Missouri during the winter of 1861–1862, remaining inactive in hopes of peace alongside other border slave states. On March 3, 1862, Maj. Gen. Earl Van Dorn assumed command and led a battle at Elkhorn on March 7, 1862, where his forces, numbering about 20,000, defeated Federal troops of 25,000 under Curtis and Sturgis. Price's Army formed the left and center, with McCulloch on the right, but McCulloch fell at two o'clock and failed to press the attack, allowing the Federals to retreat in good order. Van Dorn's forces gained control of Elkhorn. Price's Army later embarked at Des Arc on the White River, with Cousin Cæsar expressing enthusiasm for fighting in his native state. A portion of the army displayed a white feather at Iuka, symbolizing a commitment to peace, though this was considered too thin by Cæsar Simon. The army caused half of the Confederate losses and served as a sad memorial to their role. Kentucky, known as the dark and bloody ground, showed a white feather, declaring its soil a holy ground of peace, while border states withdrew from the Union and joined the South.

The steam carriage had a highly finished box, four wheels, could seat six persons, featured a pilot on top steering with a wheel, and an engineer and fireman on the aft axle, with a polished brass boiler heated by a chemical combination of phosphorus and tinder. The voice of history focuses on armies, heroes, and battles while ignoring the manners and customs of people, which were foundational to the common law of England—still relevant today as the best guide to English civilization. Sharp claims the devil never dreams, contrasting with holy men who dreamed of the Lord. The belle of Port William's heart stood in a cozy room adorned with maiden art, experiencing blushing love and feeling isolated, with no mother's smile or father's reproof, praying beneath a stranger’s roof. Sharp proposes to Conway that if Conway reveals his true name and history in confidence, Sharp will give him his own name; Conway, born in Tennessee with parents Cæsar Simon and Nancy Wade, was partly raised by his sisters and has no memory of his parents. Young Simon heard a female voice, described as shrill, say “Take Roxie Daymon away,” later revealed as his father’s dying words, and asked a twelve-year-old Black boy to point out Roxie Daymon, who responded with “good bargain, boss.” Resident pilots from Louisville were employed for navigating the falls, as pilots from elsewhere were not considered competent.

Brother Demitt, an old man known for his whisky, left Port William on foot in December, sat against a fence, fell into a stupid sleep, and was found the next morning frozen and dead, believed to have been taken by the north wind that blows because poor children are intoxicated. A council of settlers, presided over by Brother Demitt, granted preemption rights to Aunt Katy. Early preachers in Kentucky, marked by sterling piety, contributed to backwoodsmen society through earnestness and strict devotion, laying the foundation for refined society despite lacking learning or eloquence. A sermon by these preachers includes a quote from a friend echoing the idea that the Son of Man must be lifted up as Moses lifted the serpent, so that those who look upon him may not perish but have everlasting life. Don Carlo, who had saved money to buy a small farm in Kentucky, expressed a secret desire to meet a young lady who saved his life from the wreck of the Red Stone steamboat, which exploded in April and landed on Kentucky, causing many deaths. The wreck saved his life, and he later died in a saloon. A camp meeting was announced in the neighborhood of Port William, attended by old and young from ten miles around on the Sabbath.

Keel boats and flat bottom boats were the initial vessels used in the navigation of the western waters, which became a principal industry following the settlement of the West. Keel boats were propelled against the stream using long poles, with one end resting on the river bottom and the other on a man's shoulder, pushing the boat from under him. Flat bottom boats drifted with the current and sometimes carried large cargoes. A new era of free navigation on the western waters was inaugurated, though it required overcoming monopoly barriers. The Washington, built by Captain Shreve, was seized for navigating the western waters, highlighting the significance of this development.

The steamboat Brandywine was burned on the Mississippi River due to a pilot's lack of knowledge of the river, causing the vessel to run aground on a deep sand bar and ignite in the aft section under a heavy breeze. Many passengers drowned, and an Englishman survived with severe injuries, dying in a wood cutter's cabin after calling for ink and paper, which could not be retrieved in time. In Virginia, Tom intended to claim an inheritance but was not the eldest son, as Virginia law entitles the eldest son to the land estate, prompting his departure. Tom married the daughter of an Englishman, a fine gardener with no land, and received a cart-load of gourds as inheritance. Tom also owned a fleet horse and saddle, which brought him pride, but he later became addicted to alcohol. The Angel of Peace spread her golden wing from Maine to Florida and from Virginia to California.

Roxie Daymon, a handsome and interesting young lady raised and educated by the moneyed aristocracy of the city, died of cholera and left an only daughter who is now a woman and bears her mother's name. The moneyed aristocracy, which rose suddenly in the West during the first half of the nineteenth century, provided a theme for a historian and had agreed to contribute to Roxie’s expenses, which amounted to over one thousand dollars. These expenses were paid to support her company, and she was engaged by the company for several days before forgetting her letter of inquiry. After Aunt Patsy left, Roxie stopped thinking about her letter and was occupied by company until the subject was forgotten. Roxie was buried with a stone on her grave, and her fate regarding her sister remained unknown. Cousin Cæsar, well schooled in treacherous humanity, questioned the Governor about the fee for a case and used pocket-money from young Simon to pay the expenses.

On July 4, 1863, General Holmes attacked federal forces at Helena, a point three hundred miles above Vicksburg on the west bank of the river, commanding Price's infantry division (1,400 men), Fagan's brigade (1,500 men), and Marmaduke's cavalry division (2,000 men). Holmes ordered Price to attack the center fort, Fagan the southern fort, and Marmaduke the northern fort, with the onset occurring simultaneously at daylight. Price successfully captured the center fort, while Fagan and Marmaduke failed. The gun-boat shelled the captured fort, and Price's men sheltered beneath an old stump, facing an alarming scene on American Independence Day; they were compelled to retreat under deadly enemy fire. General Holmes failed to capture the other positions. Later, in September, General Price moved north, reaching Lexington on the 12th, capturing a federal force under Colonel Mulligan and obtaining five cannons, two mortars, and over three thousand bayonet guns. Cousin Cæsar, a soldier in Price's men, saw Steve Brindle, a federal soldier, and speculated about the number 77, questioning whether it meant seven men or half. Dreams are described as eddies in the mind when reflection is cut off, including images of tumbling, snakes, worms, and transportation beyond time, with one dream leading to a straw shed.
